extracted_by: hand, T-0309 — the Democrat read, December 1833
note: Vol. I No. 3, and the most consequential issue of the month: it prints the TOWN ORDINANCES adopted at the house of Dexter Graves on 4 December 1833, which appoint the town's assessor and surveyor, its collector's commission and its attorney, put four named men on a committee to contract for REPAIRING THE BRIDGES on the North and South branches, and create the WHARFING LEASE that reserves eighty feet for a street. The wharfing sections 15 and 16 are not minted here: this printing loses whole clauses of them to the column rule and the same ordinance is set again, legibly, at 1833-12-24, so they are claimed from that witness and the two printings are recorded in each other's notes (the one-list-one-cohort discipline T-0292 set for the letter lists). This issue's page 1 also carries a CLEAN setting of three standing advertisements whose No. 1 printing was unreadable — Goss & Cobb's corner, W. Kimball's New Store and A. Clybourn's market — so those are claimed here on the better witness. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST: the sweep returns eight hits and all eight are the paper's own agent list of out-of-county postmasters on page 1. Zero printed lists, zero extracted names.

The paper's imprint puts its office in the building on the corner of South Water and Clark; Kimball's New Store is on the same corner, and a January 1834 reading already in this corpus has him there still. claims.notes: THE MARKET SQUARE IS A WORKING PLACE, AND A NAMED MAN SELLS MEAT ON IT. This is the single most useful placement in the December set for a reconstruction, because the market square is a piece of PUBLIC ground the plat shows and the papers almost never populate: here it carries a butcher's market, supplied from a slaughter house and farm two miles out. The scale is worth keeping — four to five hundred hogs killed in one week, corn-fed — for a village of a few hundred people; most of that meat is going into barrels for the lake trade, not onto Chicago tables. The advertisement is the same one No. 2 prints unreadably a week earlier, where the butcher's NAME is lost entirely; it is claimed on this witness because this witness is the one that says who he is.

claims.notes: THE CORPORATION OF CHICAGO MEETS IN A TAVERN KEEPER'S HOUSE. The dateline is the claim: on 4 December 1833 the Board of Trustees sat at the house of Dexter Graves and passed the six ordinances numbered 11 to 16. No. 2 of this paper announced the meeting the day before as taking place 'at Mr. Graves' tomorrow, precisely at 2 o'clock' (1833-12-03 c004), which is how the two notices identify each other. Graves' Tavern is separately documented in this month as the landmark Matthias Mason & Co.'s blacksmith shop stands opposite on Main-street (1833-12-17 c001), so a single building in this town is the council chamber, an inn and a street reference at once. ALREADY READ ONCE, FROM A LATER REPRINT: T-0310 claimed this heading off the 1834-01-07 printing (its c001), where the house reads '[Charl]es Dexter Grave[s]' with the first name broken and supplied. This is the FIRST printing and it gives the name plainly as Dexter Graves, so it is the senior witness for the man; the January claim stands as the reprint that found it.

claims.notes: THE TOWN APPOINTS ITS OWN SURVEYOR, AT THREE DOLLARS A DAY. Ordinance 11 of the 4 December sitting. It matters to a reconstruction for a plain reason: from this date the lines and lot boundaries of Chicago are being set on the ground by a paid town officer with a name, not only by the Canal Commissioners' plat — and George W. Snow is the man whose later reputation is as the inventor of the balloon frame. The daily rate is the town's own measure of how much surveying it expected to need. claims.notes: THERE ARE TWO BRIDGES IN DECEMBER 1833, AND BOTH NEED REPAIR. This is the hardest documentary fact in the month for anyone building the river: bridges exist on BOTH the North and the South branch inside the town limits, they are in bad enough condition eighteen months before the scene date for the trustees to appoint a four-man committee to contract their repair, and the ordinance of 26 November already fined anyone who removed 'any plank or any piece of timber' from either of them (T-0308 c027) — which says they are plank-decked timber structures whose parts could be carried off. The four names are the town's merchant class: Dole of Newberry & Dole, a Beaubien, a Kimberly and John Miller. ALREADY READ ONCE, FROM A LATER REPRINT: T-0310 claimed ordinance 13 off the 1834-01-07 printing (its c004), where the column rule takes the four committee-men's names away entirely and leaves the verb as '[build]ing'. This printing carries the four names — Dole, Medore B. Beaubien, Edmund S. Kimberly and John Miller — and reads REPAIRING, which is a materially different fact about the bridges: they existed and were in disrepair, rather than being built new.

claims.notes: A BAKERY AND DRAM SHOP CALLED THE MAN TRAP, ONE DOOR NORTH OF KINZIE'S STORE, ADDRESSED TO THE POTTAWATOMIE TRADE. Three things make this the most vivid claim of the month. It names a building by its SIGN rather than its proprietor — the Man Trap — which is how a frontier shopfront was actually identified. It states its clientele: the advertisement opens 'Hoosiers and Wolverines, Behold Suckers!!!' and thanks 'his liberal patrons, the Pottawatamies', which is a Chicago business in 1833 openly trading with the Indians whose removal treaty was signed in the town three months earlier. And it places itself one door north of R. A. Kinzie's store — a relative placement in a NORTH-SOUTH direction, which means the frontage runs north-south and is therefore not South Water Street. The closing joke, 'his friends can come and get tired for nothing', is left exactly as printed.

claims.notes: A BUILDING WITH A LOT-AND-BLOCK ADDRESS, A FORMER USE AND A BRIDGE BESIDE IT. Lot 7 in block 8 is a plat coordinate — the only one in the December set — and the house on it was 'formerly occupied as a Meeting House', so the town's first congregation met in a dwelling that is being auctioned off eighteen months before the scene date. The location clause is broken exactly where the preposition stands: the transcription gives 'sie the bridge on the North Branch of Chic, River', which is either 'beside' or 'near', and neither is supplied — what survives is that the house stood at the North Branch bridge. THE SALE IS HELD AT THE EAGLE HOTEL, which is a second Chicago building named in the same notice, and the auctioneer is James Kinzie. Four wagon-loads of the sale's contents — three yoke of oxen, a one-horse waggon, harness and household furniture — are the movables of an ordinary Chicago household of 1833.

claims.notes: THE SECOND BLACKSMITH, AND THE ONE THAT NAMES THE CHICAGO HOTEL. Matthias Mason & Co. already smiths on Main-street opposite Graves' Tavern; Pierce & Abbott open this week nearly opposite the Chicago Hotel. Two smiths in a village of a few hundred, both placed by which inn they face, is a fair picture of what the trade and the street furniture of the town were. PRAIRIE PLOUGHS made to order is the product line — the shop exists to break sod for the country around, not to shoe the town's horses only. This advertisement is the first printing of a business already in this corpus's gazetteer from a later reading, so the copy date is what dates its opening: 10 December 1833.

The place the town called Hardscrabble is fractional Section 29 of Township 39 North, Range 14 East — a legal description, printed by the man claiming it, which is the strongest kind of location this corpus produces.
